plan.title: Stochastic gradient descent on a loss surface
plan.description: A ball sits on a long, narrow valley-shaped loss surface, with the lowest point marked. On each step, two arrows show the true downhill direction and the noisy downhill estimate from a small random batch. The ball then moves along the noisy estimate and leaves a trail. You can change the learning rate and the batch size, then watch the path go from a wobbly random walk to a smooth slide, or start zig-zagging across the valley.
plan.reason: You learn stochastic gradient descent best by changing its two key settings and watching the path change. You can see how batch noise and step size shape the route to the minimum.
interactions: Play, pause or advance one step at a time. The run stops by itself after 200 steps.
Drag the starting marker to a new place on the surface before you run.
Change the learning rate. Small values make short, slow steps. Values near the top make the ball zig-zag across the narrow side of the valley.
Change the batch size. Smaller batches make the noisy arrow swing more around the true one. Full batch makes the two arrows match, and the path becomes smooth.
Use 'Return ball to start, keep trail' to run again with new settings and compare the new path against the old trail.
assumptions: Illustration: a made-up loss surface with simulated batch noise, not a model trained on real data.
The loss is a simple stretched bowl: it curves 4 times more steeply across the valley than along it, and it has a single minimum.
Each noisy gradient is the true gradient plus random noise. The noise size shrinks with the square root of the batch size and is zero for the full batch.
Noise comes from the scene's fixed seed, so Reset gives the same sequence of random draws.
Readouts: step count, current loss, size of the true gradient and size of the noisy estimate. All of them describe the ball's current position.
The trail draws one marker every 4 steps, at most 50 markers; every step still runs.
limitations: Changed: the trail draws 50 markers, one every 4 steps, instead of 200; every step still runs.
Changed: the kept comparison path also draws at most 50 markers.
With noise, a single step can go uphill. The loss falls on average, not on every step.
Near the minimum, noisy runs keep jittering around it instead of settling, because this plan uses a fixed learning rate with no decay.
Real loss surfaces have many dimensions, flat regions and multiple valleys. This one has only two dimensions and a single bowl.
plan.learningGoal: Understand that stochastic gradient descent follows a noisy estimate of the downhill direction, that larger batches reduce this noise, and that the learning rate trades speed against overshooting.

draft.title: Stochastic gradient descent in a narrow valley
draft.description: A long, narrow valley-shaped loss surface, with its lowest point marked by a dark dot. A red ball is the current guess. Two arrows start at the ball: a dark one for the true downhill direction and an orange one for the noisy estimate from a random batch. Each step moves the ball along the noisy arrow and extends a thin red trail. A green start marker on the far rim can be dragged before a run. Readouts give the loss, the run status, the step count and both arrow sizes.

actions.label: Return ball to start, keep trail

assumptions: Illustration: a made-up loss surface with simulated batch noise, not a model trained on real data.
Loss = (4x^2 + z^2)/2: 4 times steeper across the valley (x) than along it (z), single minimum at the centre. The surface is drawn at 0.25 times the loss.

Noisy gradient = true gradient + noise of size 2/sqrt(batch) per component; zero for the full batch. Each step moves the ball by minus learning rate times the noisy gradient. Noise comes from the fixed seed.

Both arrows point downhill (minus the gradient), drawn at 0.15 times its size; their labels hide when the arrows get too short to name. Learning rates above 0.5 would diverge; the 0.45 maximum zig-zags but still shrinks without noise.

The thin trail passes through every step (changed from the plan's one marker every 4 steps, which would hide the zig-zag). The run stops after 200 steps (finished), at loss below 0.001 (converged), or when the ball leaves the surface (diverged).
With noise a single step can go uphill; the loss falls only on average, and with a fixed learning rate noisy runs keep jittering near the minimum. Dragging the start works while paused.

problems: assertions.2: the approved plan needs a path of at least 200 points; use a trail geometry with max 200 or more on a node

findings.message: In the default view the grey start-handle box (x=1.75, just outside the surface edge and between the camera and the ball) covers the lower half of the red ball and the base of both arrows at the initial state. The learner's first view of the current guess is blocked. Move the handle to the far side or off the camera line, or make it smaller or partly see-through, so the ball and arrow tails stay c

The default camera is low and almost along the narrow (x) axis, so the across-valley direction is strongly foreshortened. The zig-zag across the narrow side, which the plan promises, is much easier to read in the side view. A higher, more top-down default angle would show the valley shape and the path better.

Near the minimum, the true arrow (0.49 × 0.15 ≈ 0.07) and the noisy arrow (≈0.15) are shorter than or similar to the ball's radius. The 'True downhill' and 'Noisy estimate' labels point to arrows you can barely see, so it is hard to compare them late in a run. The scale is honest, single and disclosed. Hiding the labels when the arrows are this short would help.

The plan's trail drew one marker every 4 steps, at most 50. The artifact draws every step and says so in its assumptions. This is a disclosed change, and it adds to the clutter at high learning rates (see v0-s2).

Not sampled: dragging the start marker, 'Return ball to start, keep trail' and the kept blue path, full batch and batch 1, and the 0.01 learning rate. The program logic for these looks correct, but the captures do not confirm it.

At learning rate 0.45, 30 thick trail segments (each step drawn) form a dense tangle around the minimum. The ball's two arrows are buried in it, and the 'Minimum', 'True downhill' and 'Noisy estimate' labels sit on top of the tangle. The learner cannot see the arrows or follow the zig-zag. Use a thinner trail, fade older segments or follow the plan's sparser markers, and keep the labels clear of t
The 'Status' text readout (running, converged, diverged, finished) is not shown in the readout line, so the learner does not see when the run stops itself.
The grey drag handle floats in mid-air beside the surface edge, with nothing visibly connecting it to the green start cone. It looks like a stray object.
From this angle the high-learning-rate tangle is easier to read as a zig-zag across the valley, but the labels still overlap the trail.

At the start state the green start cone sits at about the same height as the ball centre (K·loss+0.19 against about K·loss+0.17), so it is buried inside the red ball. Only a green speck shows, and the 'Start (drag)' label seems to point at the ball. Raise the cone above the ball or offset it so the drag handle can be seen and grabbed.
The grey box on the far rim is the z-drag handle for the start, but it has no label or explanation. A learner will not know what it does.
The trail draws every step instead of the approved plan's one marker every 4 steps (at most 50 markers). The change is disclosed and it helps the zig-zag show, but it is a departure from the plan.

Near the minimum both arrows use the 0.15 scale: true length 0.07 and noisy length 0.15, both shorter than the ball's diameter. Their labels are hidden, so the comparison between the noisy and true arrows, which is the point of the scene, can hardly be seen in this phase. This is consistent with the disclosed single scale but weak for teaching.
The 'Status' text readout (running/converged/finished/diverged) does not appear in the captured readout line, so a learner cannot see when a run ends.

At learning rate 0.45 the thin straight trail segments form a dense tangle around the minimum. The 'Noisy estimate' and 'True downhill' labels sit on top of it, so the arrows at the ball are hard to pick out.

Not sampled: with batch 1 at a high learning rate, the noise carries the ball past |x|=1.5, and the status then reads 'diverged'. The run is still stable in expectation (the assumptions say 0.45 shrinks without noise), so 'diverged' misnames leaving the drawn surface. 'Left surface' would be more honest.
